title: The dirty pool
scenario: Riverbend Apartments CTS 40112. On Monday 5 October 2026 the committee secretary emails the body corporate manager: "The pool was filthy all weekend. Instruct the caretaker to clean it daily from tomorrow." Schedule 2 (Duties), item 14 of the caretaking agreement reads: "Pool and spa: clean, skim and vacuum weekly." The caretaker's maintenance log records a pool clean on Thursday 1 October 2026. There is no deed of variation or committee resolution changing this duty.
instructions: On these facts, is the caretaking service contractor in breach of the pool cleaning duty?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: The duty is weekly. The last clean was Thursday 1 October, so the next isn't due until Thursday 8 October. A dirty pool isn't a breach if the contract frequency is met. Daily cleaning would be a new duty, which needs a formal variation (or a separate contractor), not an instruction from the manager.
markingGuide:
Competent: Says no breach, applies the weekly frequency to the dates, and notes daily cleaning needs a variation.
Not yet competent: Treats the committee's expectation as the standard, or agrees to instruct daily cleaning.

title: The Carindale "resident"
scenario: Sandpiper Place CTS 31207. The caretaking agreement is titled "Resident Unit Manager Agreement". Clause 6 provides: "The Caretaker must be available on site between 8.00 am and 5.00 pm, Monday to Friday." No clause in the agreement, or in any variation, requires the caretaker to reside in a lot in the scheme. The caretaker lives in Carindale and attends site from 8.00 am to 5.00 pm every weekday. An owner demands that he be removed for not being "resident".
instructions: Is the caretaker in breach of the agreement by living off site?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: A title isn't an obligation. The only enforceable term is clause 6 (on site 8 to 5 weekdays), and he's meeting it. Before replying, search the whole agreement and any variations for a residence clause to be sure.
markingGuide:
Competent: Separates the title from the operative clause and checks for any residence term.
Not yet competent: Finds a breach because of the word "Resident".

title: The season change
scenario: Parkside Terraces CTS 38870. Schedule 2 of the caretaking agreement requires the caretaker to "mow lawns fortnightly from October to March, and monthly from April to September". The maintenance log records the last mow on 14 September 2026. On 2 October 2026 the committee chair emails photographs of long grass and writes: "Clear breach. It has been 18 days since the last mow."
instructions: Was a mow overdue under the agreement on 2 October 2026?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No, not on these facts.
Why: On 14 September the monthly rule applied, so the next mow wasn't due until about 14 October. The fortnightly rule only started on 1 October, which also puts the next mow due around 14 October. Either way, 2 October is too early to call a breach. The chair is applying the October frequency back into September.
markingGuide:
Competent: Applies the correct seasonal frequency to each date and concludes no breach is established.
Not yet competent: Counts 18 days against a fortnight and finds a breach.

title: The old caretaker's favours
scenario: Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731. The management rights have just been transferred to a new caretaker. The committee writes: "The previous caretaker washed down the driveway every week and collected parcels for owners. The new caretaker must continue doing this." Neither task appears in Schedule 2 of the caretaking agreement, and there is no deed of variation on file.
instructions: Is the new caretaking service contractor obliged to continue the weekly driveway wash-down?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: The new caretaker takes over the agreement as written. Favours done by the old caretaker never became duties. The committee can ask nicely, negotiate a formal variation (likely with extra pay), or get a contractor.
markingGuide:
Competent: Says no obligation because it's not in the agreement or a variation, and offers a lawful option.
Not yet competent: Says it has become a duty through established practice.

title: Strings on the sale
scenario: Bayside Lofts CTS 35560. The caretaker has applied for the body corporate's approval to transfer the caretaking agreement to a buyer. The committee writes: "We will approve the transfer only if the new caretaker agrees to clean the windows monthly." Window cleaning is not a duty under the current agreement.
instructions: Should the committee make its approval of the transfer conditional on the buyer accepting this new duty?
modelAnswer:
Answer: It shouldn't.
Why: An assignment transfers the existing agreement on its existing terms. The buyer should be assessed against the current duties only. Using consent as leverage for new duties invites a dispute. If the committee wants window cleaning, raise a separate variation after settlement.
markingGuide:
Competent: Clear no, explains assignment transfers existing terms, offers the variation route.
Not yet competent: Suggests negotiating the duty into the consent.
Source gap: The consequences of conditional or unreasonable refusal of consent aren't covered in the training. Get legal advice if the committee insists.

title: One box too many
scenario: Ocean Crest CTS 33018. You are checking the notice of an extraordinary general meeting before it is issued. Motion 3 proposes a five-year extension (top-up) of the caretaking agreement. The voting paper for Motion 3 contains the standard statement "A proxy may vote on this motion." The papers make no reference to a secret ballot or a returning officer.
instructions: What defect in the voting arrangements for Motion 3 must be corrected before the notice is issued?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The proxy box.
Why: A caretaker top-up must be decided by secret ballot, and proxies can't be used. Remove the proxy option, add secret-ballot papers and name the returning officer before the notice goes out.
markingGuide:
Competent: Identifies the proxy box and the missing secret ballot and returning officer.
Not yet competent: Says the papers are fine, or calls the proxy box "possibly an issue".
Source gap: The training states the rule but not the section. Confirm the provision before quoting it in advice.

title: The early option
scenario: Clause 4.2 of a caretaking agreement provides: "The Caretaker may exercise the option for a further term at any time." The current term expires on 30 June 2028. On 5 October 2026 the caretaker gives the body corporate written notice exercising the option.
instructions: Can the body corporate reject the notice on the ground that it was given too early?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Probably not.
Why: "At any time" means exactly that. Nothing in the clause sets a window, so early exercise is likely valid. That's the drafting risk. The fix is a defined notice window (for example, no earlier than six months and no later than three months before expiry), settled with the body corporate's solicitor.
markingGuide:
Competent: Recognises the wording allows early exercise and names the fix.
Not yet competent: Says it's too early without pointing to anything in the clause.

title: As reasonably required
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. The only cleaning duty in the caretaking agreement reads: "Clean common property as reasonably required." The lift interiors have not been wiped down for three weeks. The committee wants to proceed against the caretaker for breach.
instructions: Can the body corporate readily prove a breach of this duty?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Very hard.
Why: The clause sets no frequency and no standard, so there's nothing to measure three weeks against. The caretaker can argue it wasn't reasonably required. The real fix is a variation listing each area, task and frequency (for example, lifts wiped three times a week), with a log to check against.
markingGuide:
Competent: Explains why vague wording can't be measured and proposes measurable duties.
Not yet competent: Says three weeks is obviously unreasonable and proceeds to a notice.

title: Never done it before
scenario: Bayside Lofts CTS 35560. The proposed buyer of the management rights has 12 years' experience in hospitality management but has never held management rights. The caretaking duties include pool maintenance, gardening, minor repairs and after-hours call-outs. The committee proposes to refuse approval of the transfer solely because of the buyer's lack of management rights experience.
instructions: Is lack of management rights experience, on its own, a sufficient basis for the committee to refuse approval?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: The test is whether the buyer can perform the existing duties, shown by evidence: references, training (pool chemicals, first aid), financial capacity, criminal history check, handover plan and an interview. The committee should record its reasons. Get legal advice before any refusal.
markingGuide:
Competent: Says no and points to evidence-based assessment against the existing duties.
Not yet competent: Recommends refusal because of inexperience.
Source gap: The training doesn't cover the lawful grounds for refusal or the decision timeframe.

title: Notice today
scenario: Parkside Terraces CTS 38870. The committee chair emails: "Issue a remedial action notice to the caretaker for the gardens today. We have had enough." On Monday you requested the caretaker's maintenance log, which is due on Friday. No legal advice has been obtained.
instructions: Should the body corporate manager issue the remedial action notice today?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: First pin down the exact duty breached, get the caretaker's records, talk to him, and get legal advice. A notice that's wrong in form or substance can be challenged and set the body corporate back. Tell the chair you'll report after Friday with the evidence and a recommendation.
markingGuide:
Competent: Declines and gives the steps in order, with legal advice before any notice.
Not yet competent: Drafts or issues the notice.
Source gap: Notice content, remedy period and the resolution needed must come from legal advice.

title: The $380 drain
scenario: Schedule 2, item 9 of a caretaking agreement provides: "Minor repairs costing up to $250 per item are included in the remuneration. Repairs costing more than $250 require the committee's prior written approval and are charged at the quoted rate." Without seeking approval, the caretaker cleared a blocked common property drain and has invoiced the body corporate $380.
instructions: Is the body corporate obliged to pay the $380 invoice?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Not automatically.
Why: The job is over $250, so it needed prior written approval, which wasn't obtained. It isn't a case of paying the $130 difference either. The committee can approve it after the fact if the work was needed and the price is fair, or decline it. Remind the caretaker of the approval step.
markingGuide:
Competent: Spots the missing prior approval and gives the committee its options.
Not yet competent: Pays in full, or pays $130.

title: Tuesday afternoons
scenario: Clause 6 of a caretaking agreement requires the caretaker to be available on site from 8.00 am to 5.00 pm, Monday to Friday. An owner has recorded the caretaker as absent from 2.00 pm to 4.00 pm on three consecutive Tuesdays. The caretaker says he was buying parts at a hardware store for repairs to the building.
instructions: On the information available, has a breach of clause 6 been established?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Not established.
Why: If he was off site doing building work, that may fall within his duties. Check whether the agreement allows off-site errands for duties, and ask for receipts or work-order records for those three Tuesdays. Only then form a view.
markingGuide:
Competent: Doesn't decide either way until the agreement and his evidence are checked.
Not yet competent: Finds a breach on the owner's log alone, or accepts the excuse without evidence.

title: The CPI bump
scenario: A caretaking agreement provides for annual remuneration of $96,000, reviewed on 1 July each year by the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The applicable CPI change is 3.4%. From July the caretaker invoices $8,400 per month.
instructions: Is the new monthly invoice amount correct?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No. It should be $8,272.
Why: $96,000 × 1.034 = $99,264 a year, or $8,272 a month. He's over by $128 a month ($1,536 a year). Ask for a corrected invoice and credit for months already paid.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct figure and the overcharge.
Not yet competent: Accepts the invoice, or arithmetic error.

title: The rate
scenario: Riverbend Apartments CTS 40112. The annual general meeting has approved an administrative fund budget of $233,000 and a sinking fund budget of $78,100 for the financial year. The scheme has 1,250 contribution schedule lot entitlements.
instructions: What is the total annual contribution per contribution schedule lot entitlement?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $248.88.
Why: Admin $233,000 ÷ 1,250 = $186.40. Sinking $78,100 ÷ 1,250 = $62.48. Total $248.88. These only apply once the AGM approves the budgets.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct total, split by fund.
Not yet competent: Arithmetic error or one fund only.

title: Lot 7's bill
scenario: Lot 7 at Riverbend Apartments has 20 contribution schedule lot entitlements. The approved annual contribution is $248.88 per entitlement ($186.40 administrative fund and $62.48 sinking fund), payable in four equal quarterly instalments.
instructions: What is lot 7's total quarterly contribution?
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct quarterly figure.
Not yet competent: Gives the annual figure, or arithmetic error.

title: Ten cents
scenario: The body corporate has approved an administrative fund contribution of $186.40 per contribution schedule lot entitlement for the financial year. The four quarterly levy amounts shown on the levy schedule are $46.60, $46.60, $46.60 and $46.50 per entitlement. The scheme has 1,250 contribution schedule lot entitlements.
instructions: How much less will the scheme collect than the approved annual contribution?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $125.00.
Why: The periods add to $186.30, ten cents under the approved rate. $0.10 × 1,250 = $125.00. Period 4 should be $46.60. Fix it before notices go out.
markingGuide:
Competent: Finds period 4 and quantifies the shortfall.
Not yet competent: Says it doesn't reconcile without the figure.

title: Ten per cent?
scenario: Lot 7 at Riverbend Apartments paid total contributions of $4,620.00 last financial year and will pay $4,977.60 this financial year. The owner emails: "My levies have gone up by 10%. That's outrageous."
instructions: Is the owner correct that the increase is 10%?
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct dollar and percentage increase.
Not yet competent: Accepts 10%, or divides by the new figure.

title: Counting the cash
scenario: Riverbend Apartments' gross quarterly contributions total $77,775.00. Owners who pay in full on or before the due date receive a 10% discount, and most owners do so. The treasurer is planning cash flow on the basis that $77,775.00 will be received this quarter.
instructions: What amount should the treasurer use as the expected receipts for the quarter?
modelAnswer:
Answer: About $69,997.50.
Why: $77,775.00 × 90% = $69,997.50. Most owners take the discount, so the gross figure overstates the cash. It's an estimate: late payers and arrears will shift it.
markingGuide:
Competent: Uses the discounted figure and explains why.
Not yet competent: Uses the gross figure.

title: The minus sign
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. Lot 12 shows a balance of −$612.30 on the aged-balance report. Lot 12's quarterly contribution is $612.30. The next contribution is due on 1 January.
instructions: Does the owner of lot 12 owe money to the body corporate?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No. It's in credit.
Why: The most likely cause is that the owner has paid the January quarter early. Check the ledger to confirm, and rule out a duplicate payment or misallocation. The credit is applied on 1 January.
markingGuide:
Competent: Reads it as a credit and checks the ledger.
Not yet competent: Treats it as a debt or an error without checking.

title: Six weeks back
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The next quarterly contribution is due on Friday 15 January 2027. Under the training guidance, contribution notices are issued approximately six weeks before the due date.
instructions: On what date should the contribution notice be issued under that guidance?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Friday 4 December 2026.
Why: 15 January 2027 minus 42 days is 4 December 2026. The notice shows the amount (and any discount for on-time payment), the due date and how to pay.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct date.
Not yet competent: Wrong arithmetic or no date.
Source gap: Six weeks is training guidance. Confirm the legislative minimum notice period separately.

title: Lot 5's share
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. A general meeting has approved a special contribution of $90,000 for balcony repairs, levied on contribution schedule lot entitlements (900 in total) and payable in two equal instalments. Lot 5 has 14 contribution schedule lot entitlements.
instructions: How much will lot 5 pay at each instalment?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $700.00.
Why: $90,000 ÷ 900 = $100 per entitlement, or $50 per instalment. 14 × $50 = $700.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct per-instalment figure.
Not yet competent: Gives the total ($1,400) or arithmetic error.

title: Out of step
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. The committee proposes that the $90,000 special contribution be payable in two instalments, due 15 December and 15 March. Ordinary contributions fall due on 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October. The balcony contractor requires its first progress payment in late January.
instructions: What instalment due dates would you recommend?
modelAnswer:
Answer: 1 January and 1 April.
Why: Owners get one notice per period, there's less confusion, and arrears are easier to track. It still has money in hand before the contractor's late-January payment.
markingGuide:
Competent: Recommends aligning and checks it against when the money is needed.
Not yet competent: Aligns without checking the works cash flow.

title: Two days late
scenario: Lot 22's gross quarterly contribution is $1,382.70. A 10% discount applies only if the contribution is paid in full on or before the due date. The owner paid $1,244.43 two days after the due date.
instructions: What amount does the owner of lot 22 still owe for the quarter?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $138.27.
Why: Paying late loses the discount, so the full $1,382.70 is owed. $1,382.70 − $1,244.43 = $138.27.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct balance and the reason.
Not yet competent: Says nothing is owed.

title: Lot 18
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. Lot 18 owes $3,840.55 in contributions that are 95 days overdue. A reminder notice and a letter of demand have been sent without response. The committee meets on 20 October 2026.
instructions: Draft the one-sentence motion for the committee meeting to authorise recovery action against lot 18.
modelAnswer:
Answer: "That the committee authorises the body corporate manager to refer the arrears of lot 18 ($3,840.55 as at [date]) to the body corporate's debt recovery solicitor to start recovery proceedings."
Why: It names the lot, the amount, the date and the action. Attach an updated arrears report.
markingGuide:
Competent: Lot-specific motion with amount and action.
Not yet competent: General "recover all arrears" wording.
Source gap: The escalation threshold isn't in the training. Check the firm's debt recovery policy.

title: Put it in order
scenario: A new team member has listed the steps for recovering unpaid contributions in the wrong order: court claim; reminder notice; enforcement warrant; letter of demand; committee resolution to refer the debt to a solicitor; judgment; internal follow-up call.
instructions: Put the seven steps in the correct order.
modelAnswer:
Answer: Reminder notice → Letter of demand → Internal follow-up call → Committee resolution to refer to solicitor → Court claim → Judgment → Warrant.
Why: Nothing goes to the solicitor without committee authority, and further committee instructions are needed as it progresses.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct order, with committee authority before the solicitor.
Not yet competent: Court claim before the committee resolution, or steps out of order.
Source gap: Timeframes between stages come from the firm's debt recovery policy.

title: The treasurer's Gmail
scenario: Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731. The treasurer arranged two quotes for roof repairs ($18,400 and $21,950) by emailing the contractors from her personal Gmail account. An owner has made a records request for all correspondence about the roof quotes. The treasurer replies: "Those are my personal emails, not body corporate records."
instructions: Are the treasurer's emails with the roofing contractors likely to be body corporate records?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Very likely, yes.
Why: What matters is what they're about and why they were sent: body corporate business, sent as a committee member. Where they're stored doesn't change that. Ask her to forward the full chains with attachments for filing, and to copy you in from now on.
markingGuide:
Competent: Applies content and purpose, says location isn't decisive.
Not yet competent: Accepts that a personal mailbox makes them personal.

title: Day one of the CCTV request
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. A parked car was scratched in the basement on 15 September 2026. The building manager saved the CCTV footage from 2.00 pm to 4.00 pm that day to a USB drive; the system otherwise overwrites footage after 30 days. On 1 October 2026 the owner of lot 22, who is not the car owner, emails a request for a copy of the footage.
instructions: What is the first action you should take today?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Make sure the footage is preserved and stored securely.
Why: Nothing else matters if it's lost. Then acknowledge the request in writing, and assess record status, access rights and privacy before deciding whether to release it.
markingGuide:
Competent: Preserve first, then acknowledge without releasing or refusing.
Not yet competent: Sends the footage, or refuses on the spot.
Source gap: Owner access to CCTV and the privacy rules need advice before release.

title: It'd be gone anyway
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. Following the CCTV request from the owner of lot 22, the committee chair emails: "Just delete the footage. The system would have overwritten it by now anyway."
instructions: Why is the chair's reasoning wrong?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Because a copy was deliberately kept and a request has now been made.
Why: What the system would have done is irrelevant once someone chose to save it. Deleting material after a request is made is a serious risk for the body corporate. Keep it secure while the request is assessed.
markingGuide:
Competent: Rejects deletion and answers the "overwritten anyway" point directly.
Not yet competent: Agrees, or leaves it to the committee without advice.

title: The keen buyer
scenario: Ocean Crest CTS 33018. Your office receives this email: "I'm buying unit 9 at Ocean Crest. Please send me the last three years of committee minutes. – J. Nguyen." The prescribed fee has not been paid, and there is no written authority from the owner of lot 9.
instructions: Can the minutes be provided to J. Nguyen today?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: It's in writing and specific, but the buyer isn't the owner. You need written authority from lot 9's owner (or another eligible basis) and the prescribed fee first.
markingGuide:
Competent: Identifies both the eligibility gap and the unpaid fee.
Not yet competent: Sends the minutes, or refuses without saying what's needed.
Source gap: Who counts as eligible and the fee amount come from the current regulation.

title: Everything
scenario: Riverbend Apartments CTS 40112. Your firm has managed the scheme for 14 years. The owner of lot 31 emails: "Under my rights as an owner, provide all records concerning the building."
instructions: Why can't this records request be processed as written?
modelAnswer:
Answer: It isn't specific enough.
Why: "All records" over 14 years doesn't identify documents or a period. Help the owner narrow it with examples (minutes for 2024–2026, the current insurance policy, the cleaning contract) and a date range, then confirm the fee.
markingGuide:
Competent: Names lack of specificity and helps the owner narrow it.
Not yet competent: Starts gathering everything, or refuses flatly.

title: Where did the money go?
scenario: Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731. The owner of lot 14 emails: "Please prepare a summary of all body corporate expenditure from 2021 to 2025, broken down by category." Audited financial statements exist for each of those years.
instructions: Is the body corporate manager obliged to prepare the summary?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: The obligation is to give access to existing records, not create new ones. The five annual statements already show spending by category. Offer those as a records request.
markingGuide:
Competent: Distinguishes existing records from new reports and offers the statements.
Not yet competent: Agrees to prepare it, or refuses without offering the statements.

title: Three piles
scenario: The owner of lot 6 has made a valid records request for all committee emails about his by-law contravention. The emails fall into three groups: (a) the body corporate's solicitor's advice, forwarded to the committee; (b) a committee member's email describing the owner as "a known troublemaker who lies to everyone"; (c) emails scheduling committee meetings.
instructions: Which group can be prepared for release now, without first obtaining legal advice?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Only (c), the scheduling emails.
Why: (a) may be privileged. (b) carries a defamation risk. Hold both until you have legal advice.
markingGuide:
Competent: Releases only (c) and names the issue with each of the others.
Not yet competent: Releases everything, or withholds everything.

title: Paragraph 4
scenario: An owner has made a valid records request for a two-page committee memo. Paragraph 4 quotes the body corporate's solicitor's advice in full. The remaining five paragraphs discuss the maintenance schedule and budget.
instructions: Should the whole memo be withheld?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No. Redact paragraph 4 and release the rest.
Why: Only the privileged part is withheld. Mark the redaction clearly and tell the owner why it was removed.
markingGuide:
Competent: Redacts only paragraph 4, marks and explains it.
Not yet competent: Withholds the whole memo, or releases it unredacted.

title: Just an internal worksheet
scenario: Bayside Lofts CTS 35560. Your firm's accounts team prepared a cash-flow worksheet for internal planning. On 10 September 2026 the body corporate manager attached it to an email to the committee. An owner now requests "all financial documents provided to the committee since July". The accounts team says: "The worksheet is an internal document. Leave it out."
instructions: Is the accounts team correct?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: Once it was given to the committee it may have become a body corporate record. Include it in the assessment. Lesson for staff: don't send internal working papers to committees unless they're meant to become part of the record.
markingGuide:
Competent: Sees that sending it changed its status.
Not yet competent: Leaves it out because it was "internal".

title: The thin file
scenario: Parkside Terraces CTS 38870. The owner of lot 4 disputes a $1,200 charge for water damage repairs. The file contains: the owner's complaint email of 3 September; the body corporate manager's reply of 5 September; and the plumber's invoice. You know that the plumber's original email attached a report and photographs identifying the source of the leak, that the committee approved recovering the cost from lot 4 by VOC on 20 August, and that the owner sent a second email on 12 September attaching a quote from his own plumber.
instructions: Which records are missing from the file?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Three things.
1. The owner's 12 September email and his plumber's quote.
2. The plumber's report and photos.
3. The 20 August VOC notice, result and minutes.
Why: The report and the VOC are the basis for the charge. Don't reply to the owner again until they're filed.
markingGuide:
Competent: All three items, including attachments and the decision record.
Not yet competent: Says the file is complete, or misses the VOC.

title: The old scans
scenario: Sandpiper Place CTS 31207. The body corporate has resolved to appoint a new body corporate management company from 1 November 2026. A junior team member preparing the records handover says: "I'll leave out the pre-2018 scanned files. They aren't text-searchable, so nobody uses them."
instructions: Is the team member correct to leave out those files?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: All body corporate records transfer, searchable or not. That includes legal advice (marked privileged) and preserved CCTV (flagged as subject to a pending request). Use a secure transfer, a handover schedule and a signed receipt.
markingGuide:
Competent: Says all records go and names the controls.
Not yet competent: Transfers only current or searchable files.

title: Everything but the fee
scenario: Riverbend Apartments CTS 40112. On 28 September 2026 the owner of lot 3 makes a written request for the 2025 annual general meeting minutes and the current building insurance schedule. The prescribed fee has not been paid.
instructions: Is the request valid, and if not, what is missing?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Valid except for the fee.
Why: It's in writing, specific and from an owner. Tell the owner the fee and that you'll process it once paid.
markingGuide:
Competent: Confirms the other requirements and names the fee as the only gap.
Not yet competent: Sends the documents free, or ignores the request.

title: The report that isn't
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. An owner has made a valid records request for "the 2019 roof report". No written roof report is held. The 2019 committee minutes record that the roofer gave the committee a verbal report that the membrane was in good condition.
instructions: How should you respond to the owner?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No written report exists, but the 2019 minutes record the roofer's verbal report, and they can request those.
Why: You can't create a record that doesn't exist, but you should point the owner to the record that answers the question.
markingGuide:
Competent: States no report exists and offers the minutes.
Not yet competent: Says "nothing found" and stops, or writes up a report after the fact.

title: Which rule book?
scenario: Harbour Quarter is a mixed-use site comprising a residential body corporate, a commercial body corporate and a hotel lot owned by a separate company. Each scheme has its own community management statement (CMS), and a single building management statement (BMS) applies across all three. The boom gate at the shared car park entry needs a $2,900 repair.
instructions: Which document determines how the repair cost is shared?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The BMS.
Why: The boom gate is shared between the entities. The BMS covers shared areas, services and cost splits. A CMS only governs matters inside its own scheme, such as a residential owner's pet application.
markingGuide:
Competent: Picks the BMS and explains the difference.
Not yet competent: Picks a CMS, or treats them as interchangeable.

title: Copy and paste
scenario: A body corporate manager has taken over Southbank Junction, which has a building management statement (BMS). Without reading it, he has allocated shared cleaning costs 60/40, as he does at Harbour Quarter. Recoveries of $14,200 have already been raised on that basis.
instructions: What is the risk with the $14,200 already raised?
modelAnswer:
Answer: It may have been charged on the wrong split.
Why: Every BMS is different. Review the Southbank cost schedule now, recalculate the quarter, correct the difference for each entity and write to them explaining the adjustment.
markingGuide:
Competent: Requires a BMS review and a fix for amounts already raised.
Not yet competent: Says "check the BMS" for the future only.

title: The roller door
scenario: Harbour Quarter. The residential body corporate paid a $6,800 invoice for repairs to the shared driveway roller door. Under the building management statement, driveway costs are shared: residential 45%, commercial 35%, hotel 20%.
instructions: What total amount should the residential body corporate recover from the other two parties?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $3,740.00.
Why: Commercial 35% = $2,380.00. Hotel 20% = $1,360.00. Total $3,740.00. Residential keeps its own $3,060.00. Attach the invoice and BMS clause to each recovery.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct total, built from the two shares.
Not yet competent: Gives residential's own share, or splits evenly.

title: Expired but still billing
scenario: Your firm charges the Harbour Quarter building management group an administration fee of $1,150 per month. The administration agreement expired on 31 December 2025 and has not been renewed. It is now the start of October 2026, and fees have been charged every month since the expiry.
instructions: What total amount has been charged since the agreement expired?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $10,350.
Why: January to September is 9 months × $1,150. Those fees could be disputed. Send a renewal and ask the BMG to confirm the fees charged since January.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct figure and a plan to fix it.
Not yet competent: Wrong months, or keeps billing without raising it.

title: The wash-up
scenario: Harbour Quarter. The building management group estimated shared expenses for the year at $120,000 and recovered contributions from each party on that basis. The hotel's share is 20%, and it paid $24,000. Actual shared expenses for the year were $131,600.
instructions: What additional amount does the hotel owe at the year-end adjustment?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $2,320.
Why: 20% × $131,600 = $26,320, less $24,000 paid = $2,320. (Residential owes $5,220 more and commercial $4,060, totalling the $11,600 overrun.)
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct figure that reconciles to the overrun.
Not yet competent: Splits the overrun evenly.

title: Two out of three
scenario: Southbank Junction. The building management statement requires unanimous approval of the building management group to replace the shared fire panel ($62,000). The residential and commercial representatives voted in favour. The hotel representative voted against, saying the quote is too high.
instructions: Can the fire panel replacement proceed?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: Unanimous means all three. Get more quotes to deal with the hotel's objection, reconvene, and if still stuck follow the BMS dispute clause. Check with the fire contractor whether interim measures are needed.
markingGuide:
Competent: Says no, addresses the reason for refusal, uses the dispute clause and considers safety.
Not yet competent: Proceeds on a majority, or stops at "motion failed".

title: The fire pump
scenario: Harbour Quarter. A $2,450 invoice for servicing the shared fire pump was coded to the residential body corporate's fire safety account and paid in full. Under the building management statement, fire pump costs are shared: residential 45%, commercial 35%, hotel 20%.
instructions: What total amount should be recovered from the commercial body corporate and the hotel?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $1,347.50.
Why: Commercial $857.50 and hotel $490.00. Also recode the invoice to the BMG shared services account. Residential's share is $1,102.50.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct recovery plus the recode.
Not yet competent: Recovers without recoding, or the reverse.

title: Two votes and fifty per cent
scenario: Southbank Junction. The commercial representative on the building management group claims she has two votes because the commercial scheme has the most floor area, and that the hotel should pay 50% of a $28,000 car park repair because hotel guests use the car park most. The building management statement gives each party one vote and shares car park costs: residential 50%, commercial 30%, hotel 20%.
instructions: Is the commercial representative correct on either claim?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Neither.
Why: One vote each under the BMS. The repair splits residential $14,000, commercial $8,400, hotel $5,600. Usage and floor area don't change it. A different split needs an amendment to the BMS.
markingGuide:
Competent: Tests both claims against the BMS and gives the dollar split.
Not yet competent: Argues fairness without the BMS terms.

title: By the bay
scenario: A building management statement shares car park costs in proportion to the number of car bays held by each party: residential 120 bays, commercial 50 bays, hotel 30 bays. The car park resurfacing costs $40,000.
instructions: What is the hotel's share of the resurfacing cost?
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct share from the bay count.
Not yet competent: Uses a percentage from another document, or splits in thirds.

title: Not their pool
scenario: Harbour Quarter. The pool is common property of the residential scheme only and is not a shared facility under the building management statement. A $3,100 pool heater repair was paid through the building management group and allocated 45/35/20 to residential, commercial and hotel.
instructions: What correction is required?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Reverse the split. Residential bears the full $3,100.
Why: The pool isn't shared, so the BMS doesn't apply. Refund commercial $1,085 and hotel $620, and charge residential the full amount.
markingGuide:
Competent: Spots that the pool isn't shared and gives the refunds.
Not yet competent: Leaves the split because it went through the BMG.

title: The AGM question
scenario: Harbour Quarter. Residential owners ask why the building management group recoveries line in the budget has increased. Actual shared expenses were $131,600 against an estimate of $120,000. The residential body corporate's share is 45%.
instructions: Write a one-sentence explanation for the annual general meeting papers.
modelAnswer:
Answer: "Shared costs came in $11,600 over estimate ($131,600 vs $120,000), so our 45% share rose by $5,220."
Why: It gives the cause, the split and the dollar impact in one line. Add the main reason for the overrun from the expense breakdown.
markingGuide:
Competent: Includes the overrun, the share and the dollar impact.
Not yet competent: Gives a total with no basis.

title: Approved
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. A contractor phones about invoice #4471 ($3,280 for gutter cleaning). The invoice approval system shows the invoice status as "Approved". The contractor says the payment has not been received.
instructions: Can you confirm to the contractor that the invoice has been paid?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Not yet.
Why: Approved isn't paid. Check for an EFT entry, paid status and a zero balance. Then either give him the EFT date and reference, or tell him it's in the next payment run.
markingGuide:
Competent: Separates approved from paid and checks the payment record.
Not yet competent: Says it's paid because it's approved.

title: Right job, wrong code
scenario: Lakeview Gardens. Invoice #5102 for $1,640 from Clearflow Plumbing is for repairing a burst pipe in the common property stairwell. The work has been completed and the amount is correct. The invoice is coded to account 152 Garden Maintenance; it should be coded to 158 Plumbing Repairs.
instructions: Should the invoice be approved or held?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Approve it, with a recoding note.
Why: Holding it delays the contractor and stops the recode happening. Note: "Approved. Recode from 152 Garden Maintenance to 158 Plumbing Repairs: burst pipe repair, not garden work."
markingGuide:
Competent: Approves and gives the correct account and reason.
Not yet competent: Holds it because the code is wrong.

title: "Wrong code"
scenario: Coral Point. An approver added the note "wrong code" to a $480 invoice for replacing the pool deck lights, which is coded to account 210 Pool Chemicals. The correct account is 175 Electrical Repairs.
instructions: Rewrite the approval note so that the accounts payable team can act on it.
modelAnswer:
Answer: "Approved. Please recode from 210 Pool Chemicals to 175 Electrical Repairs: replacement pool deck lights, not chemicals."
Why: It names the correct account and number and gives a reason, so nobody has to guess.
markingGuide:
Competent: Account name, number and reason.
Not yet competent: Still vague ("please fix").
Source gap: Account numbers are examples. Use the scheme's chart of accounts.

title: "Seems high?"
scenario: Ocean Crest. An approver added the note "Seems high?" to a $9,800 invoice for lift repairs and took no further action. The contractor's quote was $8,200. The accounts payable team has asked what to do.
instructions: Who is responsible for resolving the query, and what must they give the accounts payable team?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The local team's.
Why: Accounts payable can't act on a question. The local team checks the invoice against the $8,200 quote, talks to the contractor and gives a specific instruction: hold until a set date, approve in full, or pay $8,200 pending a credit note.
markingGuide:
Competent: Puts it on the local team with a specific instruction.
Not yet competent: Leaves accounts payable to decide.

title: Mid-2024
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. An owner asks for a copy of the invoice for painting the lobby, carried out by BrightCoat Painters "sometime in mid-2024". The invoice approval screen displays only the current financial year.
instructions: Where and how should you search for the invoice?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The transaction history, set to 2024, searched by creditor (BrightCoat) or the painting account code.
Why: The approval screen only shows this year. Open the matching transaction to get the invoice, then handle the owner's request through the records request process.
markingGuide:
Competent: Right screen, right year, right search.
Not yet competent: Searches only the current year's approval screen.

title: 45 days overdue
scenario: SparkRight Electrical emails that invoice #8812 for $2,140 is 45 days overdue. The ledger shows the invoice was paid by EFT on 28 August, reference EFT-77341, with nothing outstanding.
instructions: What information should you send SparkRight in reply?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The EFT date, reference, amount, the last four digits of the account paid, and the remittance.
Why: Check those details first, especially the bank account used. Don't pay again. Ask them to check with their bank.
markingGuide:
Competent: Verified payment details including the bank account.
Not yet competent: Pays again, or tells them to check without giving details.

title: Wrong door
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. A team member trying to recode a $600 cleaning invoice has opened journal entry JNL-3302 instead of the invoice.
instructions: What should the team member do?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Leave the journal alone and find the original invoice.
Why: Journals aren't edited at this level. Recode the invoice itself and refer any journal question to accounting support.
markingGuide:
Competent: Doesn't touch the journal and refers it.
Not yet competent: Edits the journal.

title: Ten at once
scenario: Ocean Crest. A review has found 10 invoices, totalling $14,800, coded to the wrong accounts.
instructions: Should you recode the invoices yourself, one by one?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No. Refer them as a batch to accounting support.
Why: Send a schedule listing each invoice number, current code and correct code.
markingGuide:
Competent: Batch referral with a schedule.
Not yet competent: Works through them one by one.
Source gap: The batch threshold isn't stated in the training.

title: The claim
scenario: Coral Point. A $5,600 invoice from Clearflow Plumbing is for repairing a burst pipe that damaged three lots. The invoice quotes insurance claim number CLM-20419. It is coded to account 158 Plumbing Repairs.
instructions: To which account should the invoice be coded?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The insurance-recovery account, noting CLM-20419.
Why: Confirm the link to the claim first (claim number on the invoice, insurer correspondence), then recode.
markingGuide:
Competent: Verifies the claim link before recoding.
Not yet competent: Leaves it in plumbing, or recodes without checking.

title: Next to the red button
scenario: At 11.00 am on a Tuesday, a team member opens the payment system to retrieve SparkRight Electrical's remittance advice. The Tuesday payment run for 340 creditors is in progress. The remittance screen sits next to the payment controls, including "Reverse payment".
instructions: What is the main control risk in this situation?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Accidentally reversing a payment during a live run.
Why: Use view or download only. If unsure, wait until the run finishes or ask accounting support. Report any accidental click immediately.
markingGuide:
Competent: Names the reversal risk and the live-run factor.
Not yet competent: Says "be careful" with no specific risk.

title: Seeing double
scenario: Lakeview Gardens. Two invoices are received from Clearflow Plumbing, numbered #5102 and #5102-A. Both are for $1,640, both are dated the same day, and both have the same job description.
instructions: Should both invoices be paid?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No, not until you've confirmed it's not a duplicate.
Why: Same amount, date and job is a classic duplicate. Check the work orders and ask Clearflow whether two separate jobs were done.
markingGuide:
Competent: Flags the duplicate and verifies before paying.
Not yet competent: Pays both because the numbers differ.

title: GST twice
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. SecureGate quoted $1,480 including GST to replace the pool gate closer. Its invoice shows $1,480 plus GST of $148, totalling $1,628.
instructions: Is the invoice amount correct?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No. It's $148 too high.
Why: The quote already included GST. Ask for a corrected invoice of $1,480 including GST.
markingGuide:
Competent: Spots GST added on top of a GST-inclusive quote.
Not yet competent: Approves $1,628.

title: Money we don't have?
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The balance sheet as at 30 September 2026 shows "Contributions billed not due: $77,775". A new committee member asks: "We haven't received that money. Is the balance sheet wrong?" The October quarter contribution notices were issued on 1 September 2026 and fall due on 15 October 2026.
instructions: Is the balance sheet wrong?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: The line is contributions already issued to owners but not yet due, so nobody is late. Because the amount is owed to the body corporate, it is an asset. When owners pay it becomes cash; any amount unpaid after the due date becomes arrears.
markingGuide:
Competent: Plain-words explanation, separating it from cash and arrears.
Not yet competent: Calls it an error, or uses jargon without explaining.

title: Good money, a liability
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. A committee member asks why "Contributions in advance: $9,400" appears as a liability on the balance sheet. The ledger shows that 11 owners paid their next quarter's contributions before those contributions fell due.
instructions: Why is this amount shown as a liability?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The money is in the bank, but the contributions it pays for are not yet due.
Why: Until the due date, the body corporate holds it as a credit for those owners. On the due date it is applied to their accounts and the liability is cleared.
markingGuide:
Competent: Explains why it's owed and what happens on the due date.
Not yet competent: Calls it income or confuses it with arrears.

title: The $400,000 bill
scenario: Bayside Lofts CTS 35560. Cash at bank is $316,000. The building insurance premium of $400,000 is due on 30 November 2026. Other committed payments due before 30 November total $18,000. About $22,000 of arrears is expected to be collected before 30 November. The next contribution is due on 1 January 2027.
instructions: What is the projected cash shortfall on 30 November 2026?
modelAnswer:
Answer: About $80,000.
Why: $316,000 − $18,000 + $22,000 = $320,000 available, against $400,000 due. The committee must decide how to fund the gap before the invoice is paid.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct figure in a clear sequence and seeks instructions.
Not yet competent: Wrong figure, or counts the January levy.

title: The missing $116,775
scenario: Riverbend Apartments, balance sheet as at 30 September 2026: cash at bank $284,500; contributions in arrears $21,300; contributions billed not due $77,775; prepaid insurance $46,000; creditors $18,900; contributions in advance $9,400; administrative fund balance $62,600; sinking fund balance $338,675. The treasurer asks: "The two funds total $401,275, but the bank holds only $284,500. Where is the rest?"
instructions: Reconcile the fund balances to the cash at bank.
modelAnswer:
Answer: Nothing's missing.
Cash $284,500 + arrears $21,300 + billed not due $77,775 + prepaid insurance $46,000 = $429,575.
Less creditors $18,900 and contributions in advance $9,400 = $401,275, which equals the two funds.
Why: Fund balances include amounts owed to and by the body corporate, not just cash.
markingGuide:
Competent: Full reconciliation to $401,275.
Not yet competent: Says it's fine without showing the figures, or suggests money is missing.

scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The common area electricity budget for the year is $12,000. Actual expenditure to date is $24,240. The ledger shows a $9,800 payment in January for the previous year's October–December account, then quarterly accounts this year of $4,600, $4,880 and $4,960.
instructions: What is the actual electricity expenditure for this financial year to date?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $14,440 (120% of budget).
Why: $24,240 − $9,800 last-year bill = $14,440. At about $4,800 a quarter the year will land near $19,000, so next year's budget needs to rise.
markingGuide:
Competent: Strips the prior-year bill and flags the budget.
Not yet competent: Reports 202% with no explanation.

title: Off budget
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The sinking fund expenditure report shows a payment of $12,400 to RoofTech on 18 August 2026 for roof membrane repairs. The sinking fund budget for this year contains no allowance for roof works.
instructions: What should be checked first?
modelAnswer:
Answer: That the work was approved (a committee resolution or VOC).
Why: Then check the invoice matches the quote, and whether the forecast had the work in a later year and it was brought forward. Update the forecast if so.
markingGuide:
Competent: Approval first, then invoice and forecast.
Not yet competent: Skips the approval check.

title: Six hundred bucks
scenario: Ocean Crest. The cleaning budget is $48,000 for the year; actual expenditure is $48,600. The overspend is due to a one-off clean after a water leak in June. The total administrative fund budget is $640,000.
instructions: Is the $600 variance material?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: $600 is 1.25% of the line and 0.09% of the admin budget, and it's a one-off. Note it and move on.
markingGuide:
Competent: Considers dollars, percentages and the one-off cause.
Not yet competent: Flags it as a major issue on percentage alone.
Source gap: There's no materiality threshold in the training.

title: The AI briefing
scenario: Bayside Lofts. A team member used an AI tool to draft the financial briefing. It states: "Levies will comfortably cover the insurance shortfall by December" and "All arrears are expected to be collected." The next contribution is due on 1 January 2027, the insurance premium is due on 30 November 2026, and $16,500 of the $38,500 in arrears is with the debt recovery solicitor.
instructions: Why are both statements wrong?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Both are false.
Why: Levies don't arrive until 1 January, after the 30 November insurance date, so there's an $80,000 gap. Only about $22,000 of arrears is expected to be collected. Someone who knows the scheme must check every figure before the briefing goes out.
markingGuide:
Competent: Corrects both statements with the facts.
Not yet competent: Lightly edits and releases it.

title: The better rate
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The sinking fund holds $190,000 in cash. The committee has resolved to invest $150,000 of it in a term deposit from 20 October 2026. A $60,000 sinking fund payment for roof works is due in May 2027. A six-month term would mature on about 20 April 2027. The treasurer prefers a 12-month term because of its higher interest rate.
instructions: What problem would a 12-month term create?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The sinking fund would be $20,000 short in May.
Why: With $150,000 locked away until October, only $40,000 is on hand for a $60,000 payment. Six months matures in time.
markingGuide:
Competent: Identifies the shortfall and the amount.
Not yet competent: Picks the better rate without checking cash needs.

title: The low point
scenario: Lakeview Gardens. Cash at bank today is $185,000. Known movements over the next 12 weeks: contract payments of $9,500 in weeks 4, 8 and 12; a painting progress payment of $48,000 in week 4; contribution receipts of about $70,000 in week 6; and the insurance premium of $92,000 in week 10. The committee wants to place $50,000 in a three-month term deposit today.
instructions: If the $50,000 is invested, what is the lowest projected cash balance, and in which week?
modelAnswer:
Answer: $36,500, in week 12.
Why: Without the deposit: week 4 $127,500, week 6 $197,500, week 8 $188,000, week 10 $96,000, week 12 $86,500. Take $50,000 off each. The pressure point is the week 10 insurance if levies come in late.
markingGuide:
Competent: Week-by-week figures, correct low point and the main risk.
Not yet competent: Compares $185,000 with $50,000 and says yes.

title: Decide or note
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. Items for the committee's financial briefing: cash at bank $284,500; lot 18 arrears of $3,840.55, with referral to the debt recovery solicitor proposed; insurance renewal of about $88,000 due 31 January 2027; common area electricity running at 120% of budget, with next year's budget being prepared; creditors of $18,900.
instructions: Which of these items require a committee decision?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Lot 18's referral and next year's electricity budget.
Why: The rest are for noting. The insurance renewal is a cash-flow watch item.
markingGuide:
Competent: Picks the two decision items.
Not yet competent: Lists everything as a decision, or misses the referral.

scenario: The committee has invested $150,000 in a six-month term deposit at 4.6% per annum, with interest paid at maturity. The treasurer tells the committee the deposit will earn $6,900 in interest.
instructions: Is the treasurer's figure correct?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No. It's $3,450.
Why: $6,900 is a full year's interest. Six months is $150,000 × 4.6% × 0.5 = $3,450.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct figure and spots the annual rate error.
Not yet competent: Accepts $6,900.

title: Can't you just run it?
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904 is an 18-lot residential scheme. At the annual general meeting only one owner nominated for the committee, so no committee was elected. Several owners have said: "We're busy. Can't the body corporate manager just run it?"
instructions: What should be done before engaging a body corporate manager to perform the functions of the committee?
modelAnswer:
Answer: A proper push for nominations.
Why: Contact owners directly, explain that Part 5 costs more and gives them less say, explain what committee work involves, and set a deadline. Part 5 is the fallback, not the first move.
markingGuide:
Competent: Direct contact, cost and say explained, deadline set.
Not yet competent: Goes straight to Part 5.

title: Same template?
scenario: Westgate Business Park CTS 38110 has had no committee since its annual general meeting on 1 September 2026. A colleague says: "It's the same as Sunset Cove. Use the Part 5 agreement template."
instructions: What must you confirm before choosing the arrangement and template?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Whether the scheme is residential or commercial, as shown in the CMS, and which regulation module applies.
Why: The arrangement depends on the regulation module. Do not reuse another scheme's template until this is confirmed, and record the document relied on in a file note.
markingGuide:
Competent: Checks scheme type from the CMS before choosing.
Not yet competent: Uses the Part 5 template unchecked.
Source gap: Which arrangement matches each module isn't explained in the training. Confirm against the legislation.

title: Still unsigned
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. The agreement engaging a body corporate manager to perform the functions of the committee was approved at an extraordinary general meeting on 2 September 2026. The meeting authorised the owner of lot 3 to sign it on behalf of the body corporate. One reminder email was sent on 16 September. As at 5 October 2026 the signed agreement has not been returned.
instructions: What should your next step be?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Phone the owner today, then email a fresh copy with the signing page flagged and a firm deadline.
Why: Another email alone hasn't worked. Explain why it matters, offer to drop a copy round, and escalate if the deadline passes.
markingGuide:
Competent: Right signatory, phone plus email, deadline and escalation.
Not yet competent: Just resends the document.

title: Can't wait
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. The first quarterly site inspection under the Part 5 arrangement is booked for Wednesday 14 October 2026. Known issues are: cracked tiles on the pool deck; a pool gate closer that does not self-close the gate; and an overdue fire equipment service.
instructions: Which issue requires action before the inspection, and why?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The pool gate closer.
Why: A gate that does not self-close is a pool barrier safety failure. Arrange an interim measure now (for example, the caretaker secures the gate) and start the repair, rather than waiting for the inspection report.
markingGuide:
Competent: Picks the gate and acts now.
Not yet competent: Leaves everything for the inspection.

title: The quiet report
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. The draft quarterly report for July–September covers routine maintenance and a summary of the financials. It does not mention the pool gate inspection, the overdue fire equipment service, the $1,480 expenditure on the gate closer, or the actions outstanding from last quarter.
instructions: Can the report be issued to owners in its current form?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: It's missing inspections, compliance, expenditure and outstanding actions. Those are exactly what owners rely on when there's no committee.
markingGuide:
Competent: Names all four gaps.
Not yet competent: Approves it, or says "needs more detail".

title: The losing quote
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. For the pool gate closer replacement, SecureGate quoted $1,480 and GatePro quoted $1,720, both including GST and for the same scope. The VOC documentation recommends SecureGate. A colleague asks why the GatePro quote should be included at all.
instructions: Why should the GatePro quote be included in the documentation?
modelAnswer:
Answer: So owners can see the price was tested.
Why: Without a committee, transparency is the main protection. Showing both quotes lets owners check value and makes the decision hard to question.
markingGuide:
Competent: Links it to transparency and owner oversight.
Not yet competent: Says only the recommended quote is needed.

title: One pair of hands
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. Under the Part 5 arrangement, the same person engages contractors and approves their invoices for payment, with no second approver. VOC notices are issued to owners and quarterly reports are sent.
instructions: Which two fraud controls are missing?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Second approval, and separation of duties.
Why: The same person shouldn't engage and pay. VOCs and reports are good but come after the money has moved.
markingGuide:
Competent: Names both and suggests a fix.
Not yet competent: Says controls are fine because VOCs go out.

title: Saved to the desktop
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. The signed Part 5 agreement was received from the owner of lot 3 on 7 October 2026. A colleague saved it to a scheme folder on her own computer and marked the task as complete.
instructions: Is the filing complete?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: Check every party has signed and dated it, send it to the firm's agreements filing point, and get confirmation it's filed. Then note the start date on the scheme file.
markingGuide:
Competent: Signature check, correct filing point and confirmation.
Not yet competent: Accepts the local save.
Source gap: The filing address isn't in the training. Insert the firm's procedure.

title: A volunteer
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. Three months after the Part 5 arrangement began, the owner of lot 11 emails: "I've got more time now and would be happy to join a committee if that helps."
instructions: Should you tell the owner that the Part 5 arrangement must continue?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No. Welcome it.
Why: A committee gives owners oversight and usually costs less. Confirm the steps to form one and ask other owners to join her.
markingGuide:
Competent: Supports the offer and starts the process.
Not yet competent: Says Part 5 must continue.

title: The brother-in-law
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. The body corporate manager performing the committee's functions recommends a $9,000 painting quote from a company owned by his brother-in-law. He has not disclosed the relationship.
instructions: What is the problem with this recommendation?
modelAnswer:
Answer: An undisclosed conflict of interest.
Why: It must be disclosed to owners, independent quotes obtained, and the decision approved by someone without the conflict. With no committee, there's no one else checking.
markingGuide:
Competent: Names the conflict and the fixes.
Not yet competent: Approves because the price looks fair.

title: Nothing due
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. At the committee meeting on 20 October 2026, the chair proposes removing "Inspections register" as a standing agenda item because nothing falls due this quarter. The register shows the lift certificate expires on 30 January 2027 and the backflow prevention device test is due in February 2027.
instructions: Should the item be removed from the agenda?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: Two items fall due before the next quarter's meeting and need booking now. The standing item is what keeps them visible. It can be a one-line update when nothing's needed.
markingGuide:
Competent: Keeps it and points to the actual upcoming items.
Not yet competent: Agrees, or gives a general reason only.

title: In his inbox
scenario: Ocean Crest CTS 33018. The inspections register records a lift inspection on 12 August 2026 and a pool barrier inspection on 3 September 2026, but neither report is on file. The building manager confirms both reports are in his email inbox.
instructions: What exactly should you request from the building manager?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Both reports, named by date, sent to the firm's compliance reports address by a set date.
Why: A general "send any reports" gets ignored. On receipt, file them, update the register and act on any recommendations.
markingGuide:
Competent: Names both reports and dates, the address and a deadline.
Not yet competent: Sends a vague request.

title: No rush
scenario: Bayside Lofts CTS 35560. The building insurance valuation is dated 12 February 2022. Today is 5 October 2026. The building insurance renews on 31 March 2027. The committee says: "There's no rush. We'll arrange a new valuation before the renewal."
instructions: Is the committee's timing correct?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: The valuation turns five on 12 February 2027, six weeks before renewal. Get quotes for the 22 October meeting, engage on the committee's instruction, and have it done by the end of January.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct five-year date and a dated plan.
Not yet competent: Works to the renewal date.
Source gap: Confirm the five-year requirement in the applicable regulation module.

title: The valuation motion
scenario: Bayside Lofts CTS 35560. Two quotes have been obtained for a new building insurance valuation: ValuePro $1,650 and Asset Assess $1,980, both including GST and for the same scope. The committee wishes to accept the ValuePro quote.
instructions: Draft the committee motion.
modelAnswer:
Answer: "That the committee approves engaging ValuePro to prepare a building insurance valuation for Bayside Lofts at $1,650 (incl. GST), funded from the administrative fund, and authorises the body corporate manager to issue the engagement."
Why: It names the provider, cost, fund and authority.
markingGuide:
Competent: Provider, cost, fund and authority all in the motion.
Not yet competent: Missing the fund or authority.

title: Felt too high
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The sinking fund forecast recommends a sinking fund budget of $92,000 for the coming year. The committee proposes $78,100 because the $160,000 external repaint has been rescheduled from 2027 to 2029, after a building report found the paint in good condition. The draft minute reads: "The committee felt the forecast was too high."
instructions: Rewrite the minute so that it properly records the decision and the reasons.
modelAnswer:
Answer: "The committee noted the forecast recommends $92,000. It resolved to propose $78,100 ($13,900 less) because the external repaint (est. $160,000), forecast for 2027, has been deferred to 2029 following the building report dated [date], which found the paint in good condition. The forecast will be updated."
Why: Both figures, the gap and an evidence-based reason.
markingGuide:
Competent: Both amounts, the difference and the specific reason.
Not yet competent: Keeps a vague reason.

title: Nobody's tripped yet
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. A safety report dated 25 September 2026 rates a lifted paver on the main entry path as "high risk – rectify within 7 days". The committee says: "Just file it. Nobody has tripped yet."
instructions: What action should be taken today?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Get the caretaker to barrier or mark the paver.
Why: Filing doesn't manage the risk. Then get quotes this week and approve the repair by VOC.
markingGuide:
Competent: Interim measure today, then quotes and approval.
Not yet competent: Files it.

title: BlazeGuard does it all
scenario: Ocean Crest CTS 33018. The committee writes: "Our fire contractor, BlazeGuard, services all the fire equipment, so we don't need to pay for a fire safety adviser."
instructions: Does BlazeGuard's servicing of the fire equipment cover the role of a fire safety adviser?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No, unless BlazeGuard is separately engaged as adviser.
Why: A contractor maintains and tests equipment. An adviser manages fire safety compliance, training and evacuation planning. Check the file for an adviser agreement.
markingGuide:
Competent: Clear distinction and checks for a separate engagement.
Not yet competent: Treats the contractor as covering everything.
Source gap: When an adviser is legally required isn't covered. Confirm before saying one is mandatory.

title: Spot the urgent one
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The inspections register, as at 5 October 2026, shows: lift certificate expired 30 August 2026, renewal not booked; pool safety certificate expires 14 March 2027, copy not on file; backflow prevention device test due February 2027, booked.
instructions: Which entry requires urgent action?
modelAnswer:
Answer: The lift certificate.
Why: It expired over a month ago and nothing is booked. Book the renewal this week and tell the committee. Then get the pool certificate copy on file. Backflow is fine.
markingGuide:
Competent: Lift first, pool copy second.
Not yet competent: Misses the expiry.

title: The $1 million unit
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455 has 28 lots. The building insurance valuation is $28 million. The owner of lot 15 tells his bank that his lot is worth $1 million, being $28 million divided by 28 lots.
instructions: What is wrong with the owner's reasoning?
modelAnswer:
Answer: It's not a market value, so it can't be divided by lots.
Why: The valuation estimates the cost to demolish and rebuild, plus fees and site clearance. A unit's market value depends on sales, location and condition. His bank will arrange its own valuation.
markingGuide:
Competent: Explains what the valuation measures and why it can't be divided.
Not yet competent: Agrees, or gives a muddled explanation.

title: Agreed by email
scenario: Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731. On 1 October 2026 all five committee members agreed by email to accept a $3,200 quote to paint the pool fence. No VOC notice was given and no minutes were prepared. The chair asks you to engage the painter.
instructions: Can the painter be engaged on the strength of the email agreement?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: Without the required notice and minutes there's no valid VOC. Issue a proper VOC today and book the painter once it's complete and minuted.
markingGuide:
Competent: Says no and names the missing notice and minutes.
Not yet competent: Accepts the emails.

title: Seven days
scenario: Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731. A committee VOC notice was emailed to all owners on Tuesday 3 November 2026. A seven-day opposition period applies. For this task, assume the day the notice is given is not counted.
instructions: From what date can the committee decision be acted on, assuming no valid opposition is received?
modelAnswer:
Answer: From Wednesday 11 November 2026.
Why: Day 1 is 4 November, day 7 is Tuesday 10 November. Check for opposition on the 11th before acting.
markingGuide:
Competent: Correct date with the counting shown.
Not yet competent: Acts on the 10th, or no working shown.
Source gap: Confirm the counting rule and whether email service changes the start date.

title: 48 signatures
scenario: Ocean Crest CTS 33018 has 120 lots. Within the opposition period, an opposition notice to a committee VOC approving a $26,000 landscaping upgrade is received, bearing 48 signatures. Two signatures are from the joint owners of a single lot, and one signatory sold their lot in September. For this task, assume the decision is overturned only if owners of at least 50% of lots oppose it.
instructions: Does the committee decision stand?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Yes.
Why: 48 − 1 duplicate lot − 1 former owner = 46 lots. 46 ÷ 120 = 38.3%, under 50%.
markingGuide:
Competent: Cleans the signatures first, then calculates.
Not yet competent: Uses 48 without checking.
Source gap: Confirm whether the threshold is by lots, owners or entitlements.

title: Levies by VOC
scenario: Riverbend Apartments. The committee writes: "The insurance premium has gone up by $40,000. Let's increase the administrative fund contributions by VOC so the new amount applies from 1 January." The annual general meeting is on 24 November 2026.
instructions: Can the committee increase the contributions by VOC?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: Setting levies is a restricted issue for the committee and needs a general meeting. Put the extra $40,000 in the admin budget for the 24 November AGM so levies from 1 January reflect it.
markingGuide:
Competent: Names the restricted issue and uses the AGM.
Not yet competent: Prepares the VOC.

title: Four thumbs up
scenario: Sandpiper Place CTS 31207. The committee uses a WhatsApp group that the body corporate manager is not part of. The chair posted: "Shall we approve the $4,800 SecureGate quote for the gate repair?" Four of the five members replied "Agree". The chair now emails you: "The committee has approved the quote. Please issue the work order."
instructions: Can the work order be issued on the basis of the WhatsApp messages?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No.
Why: A chat thread isn't a meeting or a VOC. Issue a VOC for the quote today. Also ask the chair to export the chat for filing, since it deals with body corporate business.
markingGuide:
Competent: Refuses, gives the VOC path and deals with the records point.
Not yet competent: Issues the work order.

title: "The painting"
scenario: Coral Point CTS 29455. A draft VOC motion reads: "That the committee approves the painting." Nothing is attached. The work is painting of the stairwells, quoted at $14,600 including GST by BrightCoat Painters, to be funded from the sinking fund.
instructions: Rewrite the motion.
modelAnswer:
Answer: "That the committee approves BrightCoat Painters' quote of $14,600 (incl. GST) to paint the stairwells, funded from the sinking fund."
Why: It names the work, contractor, amount and fund. Attach the quote(s) and confirm $14,600 is within the committee's spending limit.
markingGuide:
Competent: Work, contractor, amount and fund, plus a spending-limit check.
Not yet competent: Still vague.
Source gap: Spending limit and quote numbers come from the regulation module.

title: The unfinancial voter
scenario: Sunset Cove CTS 22904. On a committee VOC to replace the pool gate closer, three of the five committee members voted in favour. One of them, the owner of lot 4, owed $1,240 in contributions that were due on 1 October 2026 and unpaid at the time of voting.
instructions: Can the motion be recorded as passed without further checks?
modelAnswer:
Answer: Not until you've checked lot 4.
Why: Confirm lot 4 was unfinancial on the vote date and whether that bars the vote. If it does, only two yes votes remain and the result must be reassessed.
markingGuide:
Competent: Checks financial status before counting.
Not yet competent: Counts three yes votes without checking.
Source gap: The effect of being unfinancial on a committee VOC vote isn't covered. Confirm in the regulation module.

title: Nine-fifteen
scenario: Lakeview Gardens CTS 27731. The opposition period for a committee VOC ended at the end of Tuesday 10 November 2026. At 9.15 am on Wednesday 11 November, an opposition notice signed by owners of 70% of lots is received by email.
instructions: Does the opposition notice prevent the committee decision from being acted on?
modelAnswer:
Answer: No, it's late.
Why: The period had closed. Even with 70% support, a late notice doesn't count. Record when it arrived, and tell the committee strong opposition exists so it can decide whether to revisit the matter.
markingGuide:
Competent: Treats it as late and still flags it to the committee.
Not yet competent: Accepts it because of the high percentage.
Source gap: Confirm the counting rule (see task 94).
